Cons:
Heater cartridge and thermistor NOT included — bought separately
No Phaetus product page or manufacturer list price — reseller prices vary ($44.44–$54.37)
Manufacturer flow figure (62.51 mm³/s) is a lab test — realistic flow ~20–30 mm³/s
Description: Compact all-metal hotend for stable, high-temperature 3D printing, rated to 500°C. The High Flow (HF) edition has a longer melt section for even faster extrusion while maintaining excellent print performance, in the same overall dimensions as the standard Dragon for zero-barrier interchangeability. Drop-in V6-compatible; includes a 0.4mm plated copper nozzle. Heater cartridge and thermistor not included.
Verdict Label: Phaetus's high-flow Dragon — 500°C, V6-compatible, heater sold separately
Nozzle Thread: M6 (E3D V6 standard); 0.4mm plated copper nozzle for 1.75mm filament included
Heat Block: Plated copper alloy heater block (custom design)
Name: Dragon HF
Mount Style: V6-compatible drop-in (with V6 adapter); rigid integral frame, one-handed nozzle change
Heat Break: Copper alloy & hardened steel bi-metal heat break, 0.1mm ultra-thin wall, with ceramic insulation below the heat break (HF) for a longer melt zone
Pros:
500°C max temp
V6-compatible drop-in, same dimensions as the standard Dragon
Longer melt section for higher flow
0.4mm plated copper nozzle included
53g lightweight

Cons:
45 mm³/s limits throughput vs UHF variants
PT1000 requires firmware configuration adjustment
Priced identically to the UHF — harder to justify unless flow is not the bottleneck
Description: The Rapido 2 Plus HF is the high-temperature version of the standard-flow Rapido 2. With a 350°C ceiling and PT1000 thermistor, it unlocks PA-CF, PC, and PEI printing without stepping up to the UHF flow rate. It's the right choice for enclosed builds where high-temp materials are a regular part of the workflow.
Verdict Label: The serious-material upgrade — same HF flow, but 350°C and PT1000 for PA, PC, and composites.
Body:
The Plus variants exist for one reason: high-temperature materials. If PA-CF, PC, or PEI are in your filament rotation, the 290°C ceiling on the standard Rapido 2 will eventually become a problem. The Plus HF removes that ceiling at 350°C.

The PT1000 thermistor is the other meaningful upgrade. Above 280°C, NTC100K thermistors lose accuracy. The PT1000 keeps precise temperature readings across the full range, which matters when you're running PA-CF at 300°C in an enclosed chamber.

At 45 mm³/s, the HF flow rate is appropriate for these materials — PA-CF and PC rarely benefit from extreme throughput anyway. For builders whose priority is material versatility over print speed, the Plus HF is the most targeted choice in the lineup.
Name: Rapido 2 Plus HF
Pros:
350°C ceiling opens PA-CF, PC, PEI
PT1000 thermistor is more accurate above 280°C
Same toolhead compatibility as standard Rapido 2
Only $10 more than the HF
Ideal for enclosed builds running high-temp materials

Cons:
Premium price at $109
PT1000 requires firmware configuration
Overkill for builders who don't push high-temp exotic materials at speed
Description: The Rapido 2 Plus UHF combines the 75 mm³/s flow ceiling of the UHF with the 350°C max temperature and PT1000 thermistor of the Plus lineup. It's the no-compromise option for builders running PA-CF or PC at high speeds in enclosed chambers.
Verdict Label: The top of the Rapido 2 lineup — maximum flow AND maximum temperature for no-compromise builds.
Body:
The Rapido 2 Plus UHF is the flagship of the lineup — the only Rapido 2 variant that combines 75 mm³/s flow with a 350°C ceiling and PT1000 thermistor. For most builders, it's more hotend than they need. For the right build, it's exactly right.

Who needs it: builders running PA-CF and PC at speed in an enclosed, chambered machine. At 75 mm³/s with 350°C available, there's no material or throughput scenario in FDM prosumer printing that this hotend can't handle.

The $109 price is the highest in the lineup but reasonable given what's on offer. The main consideration is whether you'll actually use the 350°C ceiling — if your material stack tops out at ABS or ASA, the standard UHF at $99 is a better value. But if your build is spec'd around performance materials from the start, the Plus UHF is the correct answer.
Name: Rapido 2 Plus UHF
Pros:
75 mm³/s — highest flow in the Rapido 2 family
350°C ceiling for all exotic materials
PT1000 for accurate high-temp readings
Full toolhead ecosystem compatibility
Best pick for speed-focused enclosed builds

Cons: Needs a full liquid-cooling loop (pump, radiator, fittings) — not a standalone part; industrial pricing (~$1,500+ as a kit); heavy, at the top of Prime's published 103–140 g mass range; custom mount required, not a drop-in.
Description: The liquid-cooled Mosquito Prime: the same 116 mm³/s, 500°C Prime melt zone (61 mm melt zone, dual 100 W heater cartridges for up to 200 W) with a liquid-cooled cold block instead of a fan-cooled heat sink, for printing in heated chambers where air cooling fails. Ships as a kit with heaters and sensors pre-installed, in 1.75 or 2.85 mm; requires an external liquid-cooling loop. Price basis: cheapest 1.75 mm kit variant with heaters & sensors included (100 W, 300°C thermistor, single sensor, $1,571.99). Weight: 121.5 g (midpoint of Slice's published Prime family range 103-140 g — an estimate; no per-variant weight published).
Verdict Label: Prime's 116 mm³/s melt zone with liquid cooling for heated chambers — the industrial end of the line.
Name: Mosquito Prime Liquid
Mount Style: Mosquito heat-sink mount — multiple hole patterns (top/bottom/side), no groove mount
Heat Break: Bimetallic Heat Break™ optimized for liquid cooling (copper alloy & strain-hardened steel)
Pros: Same 116 mm³/s / 500°C Prime performance as the Air version; liquid cooling eliminates heat creep in heated chambers above 80°C; no heatsink fan to fail; dual 100 W heaters and dual sensor support for redundancy.

Cons:
36 mm³/s is the lowest flow in the family — noticeably limiting at high speeds
Not well-suited for large-volume production printing
PT1000 config required
Flow ceiling becomes the bottleneck before other system limits
Description: The Rapido 2F is the compact, lightweight member of the Rapido 2 family. At 36 mm³/s it has the lowest flow ceiling of the five variants, but it pairs a 350°C max temperature with PT1000 accuracy in a form factor optimized for weight-sensitive toolhead designs.
Verdict Label: A compact, high-temp option for weight-sensitive builds — but the flow ceiling is real.
Body:
The Rapido 2F is the outlier in the lineup — it trades flow ceiling for a smaller, lighter package. At 58g versus 75g for the other variants, it's designed for toolheads where mass is a meaningful concern for input shaper resonance or print quality at acceleration.

The 36 mm³/s flow ceiling is real and limiting. At anything above moderate print speeds, the 2F will be your bottleneck before your motion system is. That makes it a poor choice for production-oriented builds or anyone printing large objects regularly.

Where it earns its keep: compact toolhead designs, bowden setups, or builders who want 350°C capability and PT1000 accuracy in a stripped-down package at the lowest price in the family. At $75, it's also the entry point if you want the Plus thermal spec without paying Plus prices — the flow trade-off is the only thing standing between you and the rest of the lineup.
Name: Rapido 2F
Pros:
350°C ceiling with PT1000 for exotic materials
Most compact form factor in the Rapido 2 family
Lightest weight — benefits high-acceleration toolheads
Lowest price in the lineup at $75
Good fit for bowden or light-duty direct drive setups

Cons:
290°C ceiling rules out PA, PC without the Plus
NTC100K thermistor less accurate at high temps
Not ideal if you regularly print exotic materials
Description: The Rapido 2 HF is the standard-flow variant of Phaetus's second-generation hotend. It handles PLA, PETG, ABS, and ASA with ease at flows up to 45 mm³/s. For builders who don't need the extreme throughput of the UHF variant, the HF offers the same build quality and toolhead compatibility at a lower price.
Verdict Label: The baseline Rapido 2 — reliable, well-supported, and a proven workhorse for standard printing.
Body:
The Rapido 2 HF sits at the entry point of the Rapido 2 family, and that's not a knock — it's a strong foundation. At 45 mm³/s, it comfortably handles everything from PLA to ABS without the flow ceiling becoming a bottleneck in normal use.

Where the HF earns its place is in reliability and ecosystem fit. The NTC100K thermistor is what most Klipper configurations expect, so setup is straightforward. Stealthburner, XOL, Dragon Burner — all compatible out of the box.

The 290°C ceiling is the only real limitation. Builders who regularly print PA-CF, PC, or other high-temp materials should step up to the Plus HF. For everyone else — PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, flexible filaments — the HF is the sensible choice and leaves money on the table for the rest of your build.
Name: Rapido 2 HF
Pros:
Excellent flow for standard filaments
Well-documented community support
Compatible with all major Voron toolheads
Affordable entry into the Rapido 2 family
PT100 upgrade available via Plus variant

Cons:
Dual extrusion is niche now — IDEX and toolchangers have largely replaced it
Bowden only; needs two extruders, two heater outputs and two sensor inputs
No manufacturer flow figure; each side performs like a V6
Water-cooled variant needs a separate cooling loop
Description: E3D's two-in, two-out dual-extrusion hotend — essentially two V6 hot sides sharing one heatsink. Each nozzle is individually temperature-controlled, so it can print two colours or two different materials (e.g. PLA with PVA support) in one print. Air-cooled as standard, with a water-cooled variant for heated chambers.
Verdict Label: True dual extrusion — two nozzles, two temperatures, one compact 30×28mm footprint
Name: Chimera
Heat Break: All-metal stainless steel (2x Kraken heat breaks)
Pros:
Two independently temperature-controlled nozzles — print two materials at once
Dual-colour or soluble-support (PVA) printing
Shares the whole V6 ecosystem: blocks, sensors, cartridges, nozzles
Compact 30×28mm footprint; air- or water-cooled variants

Cons:
Sold bare — heater cartridges, sensor, fan and nozzle all bought separately
Small-batch boutique product; availability is patchy (NorthPrint3D currently out of stock)
No verified weight published
Expensive for a bare hotend (~$115 USD at US retailers)
Fan Size: 4028 (complete kit; bare hotend ships without fan)
Description: Boutique all-metal high-flow hotend built for crash resistance: instead of a threaded heat break it uses a titanium feed tube and three titanium hollow pillar mounts, with dual vertical Ø6x20mm heater cartridges clamped into a copper melt-zone block. Takes standard E3D Volcano nozzles and mounts to Bondtech BMG-M or LGX (also Titan Aero, Hemera, Raise3D N1). Sold bare — heaters, sensor, fan and nozzle are separate purchases. Independently proven to flow over 30 mm³/s. Price basis: with terminated thermistor + heaters $160 at Advanced 3D Printing (bare hotend $115).
Verdict Label: Takoto HE20 — a crash-proof, dual-cartridge high-flow hotend for large-format builds
Heat Block: Copper melt-zone block with dual clamped Ø6x20mm heater cartridges
Name: HE20
Heat Break: Titanium feed tube; 3 titanium hollow pillar mounts (no threaded heat break)
Pros:
All-metal, tested past 320°C
Dual Ø6x20mm heater cartridges clamped for excellent thermal transfer
Independently proven >30 mm³/s flow
3 titanium pillar mounts — extremely rigid, survives crashes that would bend a threaded heat break
Standard Volcano nozzles, widely available
BMG-M / LGX mounting

Cons:
Requires water cooling — significant setup complexity vs air-cooled hotends
Currently SOLD OUT ($220 USD)
Extremely small production runs (21 units in last batch)
Solo operator — support and supply are unpredictable
Thermal conductivity ~50 W/mK (steel) — requires MPC control for best results
Limit heater to 80W during initial heat-up to prevent discoloration
No published max flow data
Description: Boutique all-steel water-cooled hotend by a solo designer. The filament path uses a proprietary hardened steel surface (not CVD) that the designer claims is as hard as tungsten carbide — enabling elastic sealing while resisting abrasive filament indefinitely. 550°C max, 39.5mm meltzone, 46g, 4x M3 Ø16mm mounting. Sold in small production batches direct via email. Currently sold out.
Verdict Label: $220 USD | currently sold out | water cooling required
Body: Now with more meltzone & less mass, v9 is back — it is made of steel and it will never wear, the filament path is comprised of materials & surfaces orders of magnitude harder than any fiber-filled filament. This means the physical dimensions of this hotend will never change. The meltzone will always remain exactly Ø1.80mm. The heatbreak will always remain exactly Ø2.00mm.
Heat Block: Steel, water-cooled block with barb fittings (3mm / 1/8" tubing)
Name: V9.2
Heat Break: Steel, Ø2.00mm bore, proprietary hardened surface
Pros:
All-steel construction with proprietary hardened surface — harder than abrasive filament fiber, never wears
Meltzone dimensions remain constant after 1000kg of filled filament
550°C max temp — highest of any currently available hotend
39.5mm meltzone length enables extremely high flow rates
Spring rate >1500N/mm — exceptionally stiff, eliminates flex artifacts
Standard M6x1 nozzle thread, 4x M3 Ø16mm mounting (Voron standard)
Free integration STEP/STL files on website

Cons: Relies on the mount structure as a heatsink — needs a metal mount with real thermal mass; industrial pricing (~$1,500+ as a kit); no published standalone weight; custom integration, not a drop-in.
Description: The conduction-cooled Mosquito Prime: the same 116 mm³/s, 500°C Prime melt zone (61 mm melt zone, dual 100 W heater cartridges for up to 200 W) with a finless conduction heat break that dumps heat into the mount instead of a fan. The fan-free option for hot enclosed chambers; ships as a kit with heaters and sensors pre-installed, in 1.75 or 2.85 mm. The mount must be metal with enough thermal mass to act as the heatsink. Price basis: cheapest 1.75 mm kit variant with heaters & sensors included (100 W, 300°C thermistor, single sensor, $1,571.99). Weight: 121.5 g (midpoint of Slice's published Prime family range 103-140 g — an estimate; no per-variant weight published).
Verdict Label: Prime's 116 mm³/s melt zone with no fan at all — conduction cooling for hot, enclosed builds.
Name: Mosquito Prime Conduction
Mount Style: Mosquito heat-sink mount — multiple hole patterns (top/bottom/side), no groove mount
Heat Break: Conduction Bimetallic Heat Break™ (no cooling fins — conduction only)
Pros: Same 116 mm³/s / 500°C Prime performance with zero fan dependency; no heatsink fan to fail, vibrate, or suck in chamber heat; suited to hot enclosed chambers; dual 100 W heaters and dual sensor support.

Cons:
No standalone complete kit from E3D anymore (configurator only)
Max flow is nozzle/material-dependent (~14 mm³/s with the stock 0.4mm brass nozzle)
PrintedSolid lists it as end-of-life (unconfirmed)
HeaterCore has no Airtable heater-type choice yet
Description: Smaller, lighter, and better than ever before, the Revo Voron HotEnd uses the smallest heatsink we've produced so far. Weighing in at only 25g, use Revo Voron to squeeze more speed performance from your motion system. Change nozzles at room temperature using just your fingers - no complex tools, no hot tightening. Revo Nozzles are a factory sealed nozzle and heatbreak in one, so they're easy to fit and can't leak material when in use. A Revo HeaterCore heats up in seconds, and its positive temperature coefficient means power reduces as it gets hotter, reducing hazards in a thermal runaway. Developed in collaboration with Team Voron; intended for use with the Voron StealthBurner, which includes an integrated cold side fan (no fan included with this kit).
Verdict Label: E3D's lightest Revo — 25g, cold nozzle changes, built for the StealthBurner
Nozzle Thread: None - RapidChange Revo system, no threaded nozzle (nozzle is a preassembled nozzle + heatbreak unit, changed cold by hand)
Heat Block: None - Revo HeaterCore replaces the heater block
Name: Revo Voron
Mount Style: Rigid mount, 4 x M3 x 0.5 bolts
Heat Break: Integrated into Revo nozzle - factory-sealed nozzle + heatbreak in one unit, no separate heat break
Pros:
25g — E3D's lightest hotend
RapidChange nozzles changed cold by hand, no tools, no leaks
HeaterCore heats in seconds, PTC safety (power drops as it gets hotter)
Developed with Team Voron for the StealthBurner

Cons:
240°C ceiling — no nylon, PC or other high-temp materials
Shorter melt zone means more modest print speeds than the V6
PTFE liner degrades if pushed past its limit
Description: E3D's entry-level hotend — 'V6's little brother'. A mostly-metal design with a one-piece stainless heatbreak/heatsink lined with PTFE, using the same V6 nozzles, heater block and groove mount. Aimed at PLA and ABS on a budget, with a 240°C temperature limit from the PTFE liner.
Verdict Label: E3D's budget entry hotend — V6-compatible, PTFE-lined, capped at 240°C
Name: Lite6
Pros:
Lowest-cost genuine E3D hotend
Same V6 nozzles, heater block and groove mount as the V6
Stainless one-piece heatbreak/heatsink is nearly indestructible
PTFE liner is cheap and easy to replace if overheated

Cons: Standalone Prime ACE sold by Slice with heaters and sensors included; needs a Bondtech LGX extruder; industrial Prime pricing on top of the LGX.
Description: The LGX ACE version of Slice's Mosquito Prime: the Prime melt zone (116 mm³/s, 500°C, 61 mm melt zone, dual 100 W heater cartridges) on Bondtech's monolithic LGX ACE cold block, giving the shortest filament path from LGX drive gears to melt zone — Slice's own recommendation for maximum flow with soft filaments. Mounts to the LGX via its interface plug; a 4010 fan cools the cold block. Note: Slice sells a standalone Prime LGX ACE (1.75 mm) with heaters and sensors included — the Bondtech LGX ACE page is a different, cheaper attachment that offers Mosquito / Magnum+ / Copperhead only, without heaters. Price basis: cheapest 1.75 mm kit variant with heaters & sensors included (100 W, 300°C thermistor, single sensor, $1,571.99). Weight: 121.5 g (midpoint of Slice's published Prime family range 103-140 g — an estimate; no per-variant weight published).
Verdict Label: Prime's 116 mm³/s melt zone on Bondtech's short-path LGX ACE cold block — maximum flow for flexibles.
Name: Mosquito Prime LGX ACE
Mount Style: LGX interface plug mount — rests at the front of the LGX extruder
Heat Break: Bimetallic Heat Break™ (copper alloy & strain-hardened steel)
Pros: Prime's 116 mm³/s / 500°C melt zone with the shortest possible filament path — Slice's own recommendation for maximum flow with soft filaments; LGX interface-plug mount, no separate mount to design; a 4010 fan is enough for the monolithic cold block; one-handed nozzle changes.

Cons: 290°C limit rules out high-temp engineering filaments, NTC100K not ideal for high-temp use, UHF nozzle ecosystem less universal than V6, Heater wattage inconsistently reported
Description: The Rapido 2 UHF is the ultra-high-flow variant of the Rapido 2, with a volcano-style extended melt zone pushing up to 75 mm³/s. Same titanium heat break and plated copper block as the HF, same 290°C ceiling. The go-to hotend for builders running 150mm/s and above on Voron and RatRig platforms. Prices vary by vendor — expect $99–$120 USD from North American distributors.
Verdict Label: The high-flow standard for CoreXY builds — 75 mm³/s ceiling with broad toolhead support.
Body:
The Rapido 2 UHF is not the hotend for every Voron build. If you're printing structural parts in PLA at 80mm/s, a Dragon HF does the same job for $30 less and weighs half as much. The UHF's extended melt zone and 80W heater only justify themselves once you start pushing volumetric throughput — which, on a well tuned Voron 2.4, happens above about 60mm/s with a 0.4mm nozzle.

Where the Rapido 2 UHF shines is in multi-material printing and draft mode. With a 0.6mm or 0.8mm nozzle at 200mm/s, the UHF stays well inside its thermal limits while a standard hotend is already gasping. The 80mm³/s rating means your slicer's speed limit is your motion system, not your hotend, and that's exactly the relationship you want.

The bi-metal heat break is worth mentioning independently. It outperforms titanium-only heat breaks at the top of the temperature range because it manages heat distribution more actively rather than simply insulating. For anyone printing nylon or ABS at 270°C+, the more active thermal management reduces the likelihood of partial melts creeping up the heat break.
Nozzle Thread: M6 Volcano (UHF) / M6 V6 via adapter
Name: Rapido 2 UHF
Pros: 75 mm³/s max flow, Detachable thermistor, Titanium heat break, Plated copper heat block, Includes V6 and Volcano nozzles, Wide toolhead compatibility

Cons:
Conduction cooling requires printer frame/mount to act as heatsink — not universally supported
Smaller community than established brands
More complex thermal setup than air-cooled variants
Fewer validated toolhead mounts available
Description: The Chube Conduction is the flagship of the Chube lineup, using thermal conduction through the mount structure to cool the hotend rather than a dedicated fan. This allows a longer 52mm meltzone and the highest flow rate in the family. It targets builders running enclosed, high-chamber-temp setups where fan-based cooling is a liability.
Verdict Label: The highest-flow Chube variant — conduction cooling removes the fan bottleneck entirely.
Body:
The Conduction variant is where Chube's design philosophy gets most ambitious. By removing the fan and relying on thermal conduction through the mounting hardware, it eliminates one of the consistent failure points in high-chamber-temp builds: the hotend cooling fan.

In an enclosed printer running 60–70°C chamber temps, fan-cooled hotends work harder and can develop heat creep issues at sustained high flow. The Conduction sidesteps this entirely — the mount structure becomes the heatsink. The tradeoff is that this only works if your toolhead and mount are designed to conduct heat away efficiently, which limits compatible configurations compared to the Air variant.

At 52mm meltzone and support for up to 47.5mm heater cartridges (higher wattage options), the Conduction has the highest theoretical flow ceiling in the Chube lineup. For the right enclosed build — Voron 2.4 or Trident with a properly spec'd toolhead — it's a genuinely interesting alternative to water cooling.
Name: Chube Conduction
Pros:
Conduction cooling eliminates fan dependency
Highest flow ceiling in the Chube lineup
500°C max temp
V6 nozzle compatibility
M3 hardware throughout
52mm meltzone — longest in the family
Up to 47.5mm heater cartridge support for higher wattage

Cons:
33 mm³/s is the lowest flow in the Slice line
Heater, thermistor, nozzle and fan all sold separately
Configurable variants make buying the right parts confusing
Description: The Copperhead is Slice's open-source, modular all-metal hotend: a Bimetallic Heat Break and nickel-plated copper block rated to 450°C, with swappable heat sinks and heat breaks to fit almost any printer. It is the budget entry to the Slice ecosystem and a popular V6-class upgrade. Price basis: Slice Standard G2 config $69.99 (heat sink + heat break + hot block), the lowest-priced generic variant. Weight basis: Standard - G2, 22 g (Slice Copperhead Hotend Comparisons table; Mass covers heat sink, heat break and hot block).
Verdict Label: Slice's affordable open-source all-metal hotend — 450°C, modular, $69.99
Name: Copperhead
Mount Style: Groove Mount or Screw Mount (G2 heat sink, selectable)
Pros:
Open-source (CC-BY-SA) modular design — swap heat sinks and heat breaks per printer
Bimetallic Heat Break, 60% better heat-creep reduction than monolithic designs
450°C covers nearly every filament
Cheapest hotend in the Slice line

Cons:
Sold as a multi-variant kit page — full-kit price not clearly listed
No verified full hotend weight published
Construction type not confirmed as all-metal by any source
Description: Mellow HeatCore 4 UHF ALPS Hotend is a compact, high-performance, high flow, high-speed front-end solution for Voron series 3D printers. It supports stable extrusion at speeds exceeding 40mm ³/s and high-temperature printing at 400 ℃. We are equipped with a complete upgrade kit and replacement parts here, with multiple optional kits to meet your needs for complete machine upgrades, partial replacements, and daily maintenance and repair.
Verdict Label: Mellow's UHF kit with ALPS nozzle leveling — 400°C, 40 mm³/s
Body: Mellow HeatCore 4 UHF ALPS Hotend is a compact, high-performance, high flow, high-speed front-end solution for Voron series 3D printers.
Name: HeatCore 4

ALPS smart leveling (nozzle-based probe) built in
400°C max temp
40+ mm³/s flow
PT1000 sensor
Complete kit with replacement parts available (Sets 1–8)

Description: The Mosquito Conduct replaces the finned heat sink with a conduction-cooled block that bolts metal-to-metal to the printer's structure, removing the fan entirely for hot-chamber industrial printing. Same 500°C Bimetallic Heat Break and melt zone as the air-cooled Mosquito. Professional installation only. Price basis: Slice Kit $199.99 (single variant). Weight: 41 g (Slice product page, Technical Specifications table).
Verdict Label: Fan-free Mosquito for enclosed industrial printers — conduction cooling, 500°C

Same 500°C melt zone as the standard Mosquito

Description: BRS Engineering's Dragon Ultra CF is a Dragon-structure hotend rebuilt for carbon-fiber filaments: a custom composite ceramic heat break with ceramic ring insulation, a Volcano-style copper-plated or aluminum block, and a 70W cartridge heater with PT1000 sensor, assembled and torqued by BRS. An M6 extender lets it run V6 nozzles, and a tungsten carbide nozzle is optional. Price basis: BRS list €215 (converted, $239.53); the lowest BRS variant is €108 but its configuration is unlabeled.
Verdict Label: BRS's carbon-fiber-proof Dragon — ceramic composite heat break, PT1000, built for PA-CF
Nozzle Thread: M6 Volcano (V6 via included M6 extender)
Heat Block: Volcano-style copper-plated or aluminum heat block
Name: Dragon Ultra CF
Heat Break: Composite ceramic heat break, ceramic ring insulation

Custom composite ceramic heat break tested 100kg+ PA12-CF15 over 12 months without failure
Volcano block with optional fully-machined tungsten carbide nozzle
PT1000 sensor; Dragon-pattern mount fits standard toolheads

Cons:
35 mm³/s flow is modest by 2026 standards
Heater cartridge, thermistor and fan sold separately
Kit with nozzle, boot and paste costs more than the hotend alone
Description: Slice Engineering's original Mosquito is a compact, lightweight all-metal hotend built around a Bimetallic Heat Break and a nickel-plated copper alloy hot block rated to 500°C. Its rigid roll-cage heat sink protects the thin-walled heat break and enables one-handed nozzle changes, while the 37g mass keeps toolhead weight minimal. Uses RepRap-style M6 nozzles and a 50W cartridge heater. Price basis: Fabreeko Barebones ($104.99), the lowest-end config; the Kit with GammaMaster nozzle, silicone boot and paste is $149.99.
Verdict Label: The original lightweight all-metal hotend — 500°C, 37g, one-handed nozzle changes
Name: Mosquito

Featherweight 37g — fastest accelerations in its class

Fan not included — requires separate sourcing and mounting

Description: The Goliath is a high-flow hotend designed by the VzBoT team and manufactured by Mellow. It features a 50mm meltzone, nickel-plated copper heat block with a 100W 24V nichrome wire heater, and a bi-material copper-zirconia heatbreak. Mounting pattern matches the Dragon hotend, giving it broad toolhead compatibility.
Verdict Label: A VzBoT-designed extreme-flow hotend — unmatched meltzone at this price, but not a beginner install.
Body:
The Goliath is the hotend the VzBoT team built because nothing else was fast enough for their printer. A 50mm meltzone paired with a 100W nichrome heater and a 550°C ceiling puts it in a different category than anything Phaetus or E3D offers at this price point. On AliExpress it regularly lands under $35.

The Dragon-compatible mount pattern is the key to its wide adoption. It drops into Stealthburner, XOL, Dragon Burner, and most toolheads with minimal modification. That's a significant advantage for a hotend with this kind of spec.

The installation experience is less polished than a Rapido 2. The nichrome wire needs to be routed and bent carefully — do it wrong and the wire fatigues and breaks. The PT1000 M3 thread strips easily if you overtighten. The fan is not included and needs to be sourced and mounted separately. These are manageable for an experienced builder but worth knowing before you order.

For VzBoT users it's the obvious choice. For Voron builders willing to do the setup work, it's one of the best value high-flow options available.
Name: Goliath Air
Pros:
50mm meltzone — longest in any air-cooled prosumer hotend
550°C maximum temp ceiling
100W 24V nichrome heater for fast ramp times
Dragon-compatible mounting pattern — broad toolhead support
V6 nozzle thread
Bi-material copper-zirconia heatbreak
Open-source design by VzBoT team

Cons:
Requires a full water cooling loop — significant added complexity and cost
Nichrome wire routing still requires care
Silicone sock only rated to 300°C
M3 thermistor thread strips easily
Not practical for most standard Voron builds without significant modification
Description: The Goliath Water is the liquid-cooled variant of the VzBoT Goliath, replacing the air-cooled aluminum heatsink with a water-cooled block and included fittings. All other specs are identical to the Air variant. It enables sustained extreme flow rates that air cooling cannot support at prolonged high speeds.
Verdict Label: The water-cooled Goliath unlocks the full meltzone potential — for builds already running liquid cooling.
Body:
The Goliath Water is the same hotend as the Air variant with the heatsink swapped out for a water block and fittings. Everything else — meltzone, heater, heatbreak, nozzle thread, mount pattern — is identical.

The reason to choose it over the Air is sustained high-speed printing. Air cooling works until chamber temps climb or print speeds push sustained flow rates past what the heatsink can dissipate. Water cooling removes that ceiling. For VzBoT builds or any printer already running a water cooling loop, it's the natural choice.

For standard Voron builds that aren't already water-cooled, the infrastructure cost is significant. A pump, reservoir, radiator, tubing, and fittings add complexity and cost that most builders don't have headroom for. The Air variant covers the vast majority of use cases. The Water variant is for builds where it doesn't.
Name: Goliath Water
Pros:
Water cooling removes the thermal limit of air-cooled heatsink
Highest sustained flow ceiling of any listed hotend
550°C max temp
100W 24V nichrome heater
Water fittings included
Dragon-compatible mount
Open-source design

Cons:
100W dual-heater config is professional-install only (fire/burn warnings apply)
Heaters and sensors sold separately — bundles run $300+
73g and 60mm tall — heavier and taller than the Mosquito/Magnum
Description: The Magnum+ is Slice's industrial high-flow Mosquito, with an extended melt zone that reaches 90 mm³/s and two heater sockets for up to 100W. It keeps the 500°C rating, Bimetallic Heat Break and one-handed nozzle changes of the line, in a taller 73g frame available for 1.75 and 2.85mm filament. Price basis: Fabreeko bundle $249.99 (unassembled, no heater or sensor); Slice Bundle from $299.99.
Verdict Label: Slice's industrial high-flow hotend — 90 mm³/s, 500°C, up to 100W
Name: Mosquito Magnum+
Mount Style: Rigid mount — M2.5 tapped holes on heat sink (adapter/printed mount)
Pros:
90 mm³/s flow — 2.5x the standard Mosquito
Dual 50W heater sockets for up to 100W
500°C rating, 1.75 and 2.85mm filament
Same Bimetallic Heat Break and roll-cage one-handed nozzle change

Cons:
Requires mount/toolhead designed to conduct heat away efficiently
Smaller compatible toolhead set than air variant
Fewer community examples of completed conduction builds
Sourcing 4mm heater cartridges requires planning
Description: The Tricorn Conduction replaces the active heatsink fan with thermal conduction through the mounting structure, identical to the Chube Conduction approach. All other specs match the Tricorn Air — inverted heatbreak, 3x 40W 4mm cartridges, Dragon mount, M3/M4 hardware, 500°C ceiling. The long meltzone variant measures 53.5mm with nozzle.
Verdict Label: Same Tricorn hardware, fan dependency removed — best for high-temperature enclosed builds.
Body:
The Tricorn Conduction is the same hotend as the Air variant with the active heatsink replaced by a conduction cooling block that transfers heat through the toolhead mount structure. For builders running high-chamber-temperature enclosures — 60°C and above — it eliminates the most common thermal failure mode: the heatsink fan struggling against ambient heat.

The tradeoff is that conduction cooling only works as well as the mount design allows. The toolhead and carriage need to be spec'd for it. There are fewer validated configurations than the air variant, and the community examples are more sparse. This is a more specialized install than the standard Tricorn Air.

Where it earns its place is exactly where the Chube Conduction earns its: enclosed Voron builds with elevated chamber temps and a builder who wants to eliminate the fan as a variable. At roughly the same price as other conduction-cooled options from more established brands, the Tricorn Conduction offers a genuinely novel heatbreak geometry that competitors don't match.
Name: Tricorn Conduction
Pros:
Eliminates heatsink fan dependency
Ideal for 60–70°C enclosed chambers
500°C component temp ceiling
Inverted heatbreak geometry
3x 40W 4mm heater cartridges
M3/M4 hardware only
Dragon-compatible mount
Highest flow ceiling in the Tricorn lineup

Cons:
Newer brand with smaller install base than Phaetus
Fewer documented Klipper configs in the wild
4mm heater cartridges are less commonly stocked than 6mm
Open-source license is CC BY-NC — commercial use requires a separate license
Description: The Tricorn is an open-source hotend designed around an inverted heatbreak geometry, three 40W 4mm heater cartridges, and Dragon-compatible mounting. It comes in air-cooled and conduction-cooled variants with long (53.5mm) and short (41mm) meltzone options. Hardware is M3/M4 throughout.
Verdict Label: An open-source hotend that re-thinks the heat block from first principles — and mostly gets it right.
Body:
The Tricorn gets noticed because it does something unusual: it inverts the heatbreak so the threads sit outside the melt zone rather than inside it. The practical result is better thermal isolation and a cleaner boundary between the cold and hot zones. It's not a marginal improvement — it changes the geometry of heat transfer in a way that most conventional hotend designs don't address.

The heater arrangement is equally unconventional. Three 40W 4mm cartridges instead of one 6mm cartridge. The combined surface area is higher, the wattage headroom is substantial, and if one cartridge fails you still have two. 4mm cartridges are less commonly stocked at general electronics suppliers, which is the main sourcing consideration.

The M3/M4 hardware-only rule is a quality-of-life decision that experienced builders will appreciate immediately. No M2.5 screws to strip. No M1.6 anything. Every fastener on the unit is a size that most builders already own drivers for.

The air-cooled variant is the standard install. The conduction variant is for enclosed high-temperature builds where chamber temperatures make fan-cooled heatsinks work harder than they should. Both share the same Dragon-compatible mount, so existing toolhead mounts work without modification.

The project is open-source under CC BY-NC 4.0, manufactured by Excit3D, Fabreeko, and Lettucehead3D. Physical units are vendor-specific in some details — check your vendor's spec sheet before ordering.
Name: Tricorn Air
Pros:
500°C component temp ceiling
Inverted heatbreak keeps threads out of melt zone
3x 40W 4mm heater cartridges — higher combined surface area than a single 6mm
M3/M4 hardware only — no tiny screws
Dragon-compatible mount
Air or conduction cooled variants
Open-source design (CC BY-NC 4.0)
Passive heatsink holds 118°C with block at 260°C uncooled

Cons:
Modest ~15 mm³/s flow — outclassed for speed by modern high-flow hotends
Kit requires assembly (pre-assembled costs more)
Supplied thermistor caps at 300°C; higher temps need PT100/PT1000 + copper block
Description: E3D's original all-metal hotend and the design most of the industry copied. All-metal heat break, cartridge heater block, groove mount, 300°C with the supplied thermistor (up to 500°C with a PT100/PT1000 and plated copper block). Weight: 26 g per the Voron3D Wiki specs table (E3D publishes no weight).
Verdict Label: The all-metal standard every other hotend is measured against — 300°C, M6 nozzles, endless mounts
Name: V6
Pros:
300°C all-metal design
M6 nozzle ecosystem — the de-facto standard
Groove mount fits nearly every toolhead
Proven, reliable, huge community support

Cons:
Single 50W heater ceiling — no dual-heater option
Heater, thermistor and fan sold separately
Modest flow gain over the standard Mosquito for the price
Description: The Mosquito Magnum adds an extended melt zone and a thermal insulator to the original Mosquito, lifting flow to 40 mm³/s in the same 41g, 500°C package. Same Bimetallic Heat Break, nickel-plated copper block and roll-cage frame, so it drops into any Mosquito mount or adapter. Price basis: Fabreeko Barebones ($129.99), the lowest-end config; the Kit with nozzle, boot and paste is $174.99.
Verdict Label: The high-flow Mosquito — 40 mm³/s in the same 41g footprint
Name: Mosquito Magnum
Mount Style: Rigid mount — pairs of M2.5 tapped holes, heat sink top & bottom
Pros:
Extended melt zone pushes flow to 40 mm³/s
Same 41g mass and 500°C rating as the original Mosquito
Thermal insulator protects the melt zone from cooling losses
Drop-in for Mosquito mounts and adapters

Cons: No heatsink fan included (Mellow recommends a fan ≥40 mm); no published weight, dimensions, or nozzle thread; limited community build data vs Goliath line; niche dual-feed product for large-format builds
Fan Size: None - no fan included (>=40 mm recommended)
Description: Mellow3D all-metal integrated hotend designed for large-format and high-speed 3D printers. The 'Air' designation indicates air-cooled heatsink (vs water-cooled). 'Lite' indicates a reduced-weight variant. Part of the DualVelo product family. All-metal construction with no PTFE in the melt zone. Dual-feed, single-nozzle design for multi-colour/material blending; the kit includes the extruder (36 mm motor, NF hardened-steel gears), 2× 24 V 60 W heaters, a PT1000 sensor, and 0.4 + 0.6 mm brass nozzles; no fan included. Price basis: regular kit price $276 (flash sale $143.52 at time of check, temporary).
Verdict Label: Mellow's large-format hotend-and-extruder unit — $129, specs thin on the ground
Name: DualVelo Air Lite
Heat Break: Aerospace-grade low-friction wear tube core; titanium alloy reinforcement screws
Pros: All-metal construction, air-cooled (no liquid cooling required), Mellow3D quality manufacturing, designed for high-speed operation

Cons:
Heater cartridge and thermistor NOT included — bought separately
500°C needs PT1000/thermocouple-class sensing and suitable firmware, not the stock NTC setup
Longer than a standard Dragon — check toolhead clearance
Description: Phaetus's ultra-high-flow Dragon. A lengthened plated-copper heat block plus an extended nut stretch the melt zone for up to 70.5 mm³/s, while a 0.25mm-wall titanium heat break keeps heat where it belongs. All-metal, 500°C-capable, V6-nozzle compatible and a drop-in for V6/Dragon mounts. Heater cartridge and thermistor are not included.
Verdict Label: Phaetus's ultra-high-flow Dragon — 70.5 mm³/s, 500°C, V6-compatible drop-in
Name: Dragon UHF
Pros:
70.5 mm³/s — the highest-flow Dragon
500°C all-metal design for PEEK/PEI and other engineering filaments
Thin-wall (0.25mm) titanium heat break for excellent thermal isolation
V6 nozzle ecosystem and one-handed nozzle changes
Light at 61.2g

Cons: Longer heat block can cause stringing with slow retraction, requires Volcano nozzles (larger selection than V6 but still limited), community price page returned 404 — price needs verification
Description: Triangle Lab's Compact High Conduction XL — a Volcano-format all-metal hotend. Extends the CHC Pro design with a longer heat block for higher flow using large-format or Volcano nozzles. All-metal construction with no PTFE in the melt zone. Compatible with standard V6 heaters and cartridges. Popular in the VzBot community for high-temp, high-flow printing.
Verdict Label: Trianglelab's ceramic high-flow hotend — air or water cooled, 48g
Body: The CHC® XL is a high flow hot end designed specifically for high speed FDM printing. It has a lightweight design with ceramic heating elements to reduce dead weight at high speeds. It is compact and ruggedized to reduce your cost of operation.
Name: CHC XL
Heat Break: Patented multiple thermal break design; monolithic construction
Pros: All-metal melt zone, Volcano nozzle compatibility for very high flow, well-priced for performance, proven Triangle Lab manufacturing

Cons:

Ceramic plate heater is a newer design with less long-term history than cartridges
Often sold out at major retailers
Description: Phaetus's (DropEffect) neXt G extreme-gradient hotend, successor to the XG. A ceramic heating plate and a long melt zone deliver up to 45 mm³/s with the UHF groove adapter, while a rigid kinematic coupling keeps the heater block stiff and isolates the heatsink. Same dimensions as the Dragon hotend and compatible with V6 nozzles. This red version uses a 104NT thermistor (280°C+).
Verdict Label: Phaetus's extreme-gradient Dragon-footprint hotend — 45 mm³/s, kinematic coupling, V6 nozzles
Name: NexG
Pros:
45 mm³/s with the UHF groove adapter
Kinematic coupling — rigid block, minimal heat transfer to the heatsink
Same footprint as the Dragon, so it drops into Dragon toolheads

Description: The Mosquito Liquid swaps the finned heat sink for a corrosion-resistant bronze liquid-cooling block, so it keeps printing in heated chambers above 80°C where fan-cooled hotends fail. Same 500°C Bimetallic Heat Break and nickel-plated copper block as the standard Mosquito, with a conduction-optimized heat break. Fittings sold separately (G1/8 Eisele). Price basis: Slice Kit $189.99 (single variant).
Verdict Label: The Mosquito for heated chambers — liquid-cooled, 500°C, 74g
Name: Mosquito Liquid
Mount Style: Rigid mount — M2.5 tapped holes on liquid-cooled bronze base
Pros:
Liquid cooling works in 80°C+ chambers where fans fail
Corrosion-resistant bronze base suits most coolants
Same 500°C Bimetallic Heat Break technology as the air-cooled Mosquito
Ships with GammaMaster nozzle and boron nitride paste

Cons: Extremely expensive (~$1,570+ as a kit); overkill for any hobbyist build — aimed at industrial users; large and heavy (103 g, 88 mm tall); needs a 24 V system and a custom mount; heatsink fan not included.
Description: Slice Engineering's air-cooled Mosquito Prime: the world's highest-flow production hotend, with a 61 mm melt zone, dual 100 W (24 V) heater cartridges for up to 200 W, and a 500°C nickel-plated copper-alloy hot block. Rated 116 mm³/s with PLA (64 mm³/s TPU) using a 1.4 mm nozzle; ships as a kit with heaters and sensors pre-installed, in 1.75 or 2.85 mm. The heat sink takes a 25 mm fan; the 103 g figure is the 1.75 mm air-cooled mass. Price basis: cheapest 1.75 mm kit variant (100 W, 300°C thermistor, single sensor, $1,571.99) — 2.85 mm and 200 W / dual-sensor variants cost more.
Verdict Label: The world's highest-flow hotend — 116 mm³/s, 500°C, and an industrial price tag to match.
Name: Mosquito Prime Air
Mount Style: Mosquito heat-sink mount — multiple hole patterns (top/bottom/side), no groove mount
Heat Break: Bimetallic Heat Break™ (copper alloy & strain-hardened steel)
Pros: Highest rated volumetric flow of any production hotend (116 mm³/s PLA); 500°C nickel-plated copper-alloy hot block; 61 mm melt zone gives a consistent melt at extreme flow; dual heaters and dual sensors (up to 200 W); one-handed nozzle changes; made in the USA with strong support.

Sold bare in the cheapest variant — heaters, sensor, fan and nozzle bought separately
No verified weight published

Description: Longer variant of the Takoto HE20: the melt zone is extended 3 times for even higher flow, independently proven over 50 mm³/s (HartSmart: over 55 with PLA+, 1.0 mm nozzle). Same crash-resistant construction as the HE20 — a titanium feed tube and three titanium hollow pillar mounts, with dual vertical Ø6x20mm heater cartridges clamped into a copper melt-zone block. Takes E3D Supervolcano nozzles and mounts to Bondtech BMG-M or LGX (also Titan Aero, Hemera, Raise3D N1; Multi-Mount option). Sold bare — heaters, sensor, nozzle and fan are separate purchases. Price basis: with-heaters variant $210 at Advanced 3D Printing (BMG mount; bare hotend $180).

Heat Block: Copper melt-zone block, 3x the HE20 melt zone, with dual clamped Ø6x20mm heater cartridges
Name: HE50

Pros:
All-metal, tested past 320°C
Dual Ø6x20mm heater cartridges clamped for excellent thermal transfer
Independently proven >50 mm³/s flow (HartSmart: >55)

Description: The fiber-optimized version of Phaetus's (DropEffect) neXt G extreme-gradient hotend. Same 45 mm³/s UHF flow and rigid kinematic coupling as the standard neXt G, but with a PT1000 thermistor (320°C+), an RCC-coated all-metal heat break, and hardened steel nozzles for abrasive fiber-filled filaments like PA-CF and PET-CF.
Verdict Label: The fiber-printing neXt G — 45 mm³/s, PT1000, hardened steel nozzles, RCC-coated heat break
Name: neXt G Fiber
Pros:
Built for fiber-filled filaments — hardened steel nozzles included (0.4 + 0.5mm)
PT1000 thermistor for 320°C+ printing

Cons:
Newer brand with smaller community footprint than Phaetus or E3D
Limited reseller network
Air cooling requires fan mounting solution not included
Fewer documented Klipper config examples
Description: The Chube Air is a high-flow, air-cooled hotend from Luke's Lab designed around V6 nozzle compatibility and all M3 hardware. With a 500°C max temp ceiling and a 42mm meltzone, it targets prosumer builders who want extreme temperature headroom without proprietary nozzle lock-in.
Verdict Label: A genuinely original high-flow design — impressive specs, but ecosystem support is still maturing.
Body:
The Chube Air makes a strong first impression on paper: 500°C ceiling, V6 nozzle compatibility, all M3 hardware, and a 42mm meltzone. For builders frustrated by proprietary nozzle systems or tiny M2.5 screws that strip on the third swap, Chube's design philosophy directly addresses real pain points.

The V6 compatibility is the most practically meaningful feature. Your existing nozzle library works. Brass, hardened, CHT variants — they all thread in. The same applies to heater cartridges and the 3x15mm thermistor sensor, which is the standard form factor most Voron builders already stock.

The gap right now is ecosystem maturity. Phaetus and E3D have years of community configs, mounting solutions, and documented quirks. Chube is newer, the reseller network is thinner, and there are fewer Klipper config examples to pull from. For early adopters willing to do some groundwork, the hardware is legitimately interesting. For builders who want a plug-and-play experience, the Rapido 2 family is still the safer bet.
Name: Chube Air
Pros:
500°C max temp — highest ceiling in its class
V6 nozzle compatibility — use your existing stock
M3 hardware throughout — no tiny screws to strip
Standard 3x15mm thermistor cartridge
6x20–22mm heater cartridge compatibility
42mm meltzone length

Cons: Preorder / limited initial availability, performance data still emerging from community, premium price vs Rapido 2 line
Description: Phaetus' next-generation high-flow hotend successor to the Rapido 2. Features an EndCoat titanium alloy heatbreak for reduced heat creep, copper alloy heating block for improved thermal mass, and an aluminum heatsink. Rated for over 100 mm³/s flow and up to 1300 mm/s print speeds per Phaetus claims. V6 nozzle compatible.
Verdict Label: Phaetus's highest-flow Rapido — 103 mm³/s with a 120W ceramic heater
Body: Liber™ heats and melts filament faster and more thoroughly, providing a consistent material supply for high-speed, high-flow extrusion.
Name: Rapido X
Mount Style: Standard 16mm bolt-hole mounting; also compatible with GrooveMount quick-release interface
Pros: Highest-flow Phaetus offering, EndCoat heatbreak reduces jamming, V6 nozzle ecosystem, strong community anticipation

Cons:
45 mm³/s is the lowest flow in the Chube family
33mm meltzone is shorter than Air and Conduction
Smaller community and fewer validated configs
Not ideal for high-speed production printing
Description: The Chube Compact is the smallest member of the Chube family, with a 22.23mm OD and 48.5mm length. It uses a 6x16mm heater cartridge (upgradeable to 6x20mm) and a 33mm meltzone. Designed for toolhead designs where space and mass are a constraint but 500°C headroom is still desired.
Verdict Label: A compact V6-compatible hotend with 500°C headroom — best for weight-sensitive toolheads.
Body:
The Chube Compact occupies the same niche as the Rapido 2F — small, light, still capable of high temperatures — but with V6 nozzle compatibility as the differentiator. At 22.23mm OD it fits toolhead designs that the larger Air and Conduction variants can't.

The 33mm meltzone and 45 mm³/s ceiling are real limitations. This isn't a high-throughput hotend. But if your use case is a compact toolhead on a Voron running standard materials at moderate speed with occasional high-temp filament (PA, PC), the 500°C ceiling gives you that headroom without needing a larger body.

At $65 it's the entry point into the Chube family and the easiest to justify as a trial. If Chube's V6-native approach appeals to you, the Compact is the lowest-risk way to evaluate it before committing to the Air or Conduction variants.
Name: Chube Compact
Pros:
Smallest form factor in the Chube lineup
500°C max temp ceiling
V6 nozzle compatibility
M3 hardware throughout
Lowest price in the Chube family
22.23mm OD — drops into tight toolhead spaces
